catalog_quote: Stress is not being analyzed as phonemic, as it is not contrastive. However there are complications in discerning stress because pitch, length, and/or intensity do not function together. There is a strong tendency to stress the last syllable in any word, and in words of more than two syllables there may be one or two secondarily-stressed syllables, most frequently alternating secondary-stress and unstressed. Stress can shift with affixation and/or adjust to the stress pattern of the following word or morpheme. Reduplicated words tend to be stressed equally. ... new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog final stress (final stress) — agrees — and adds that stress is non-contrastive, that secondary stresses alternate leftward from the final syllable, that stress shifts onto the clitic -el and adjusts to the following word, that reduplications are evenly stressed, and that there is no tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the last syllable of the word ('strong tendency'); it is realised by pitch rise, length and/or 'ballistic' intensity, which do not always coincide. No tone. Examples: [ˌɑ.ˈpul] 'to do', [ɑi.ˌɛk.wɑi.ˈjo] 'to mock', [ɑ.ˈᵑgɑi] 'tomorrow', [ɑ.ˌko.pi.ˈtɛkŋ] 'small', [ˌkuɾ.ˈkwɑn], [ˌkɾɑ.ˈtɛmpʰ].
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'in words of more than two syllables there may be one or two secondarily-stressed syllables, most frequently alternating secondary-stress and unstressed' (i.e. alternating leftward from the final primary, e.g. [ɑ.ˌko.pi.ˈtɛkŋ] 'small', [ˌt̚n̥nĩ.mboi.ˈɛl] 'new').
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts with affixation and clitics: [ɑ.ˈᵑgɑi] 'tomorrow' vs [ˌɑ.ᵑgɑi.ˈɛl] 'tomorrow-(dep.cl.)', where primary stress moves to the clitic -el and the first syllable takes secondary stress; stress may adjust to the following word/morpheme; reduplicated words tend to be stressed equally; in some words the cues split across two syllables (e.g. [ˌɑ.ˈpul]: vowel length on syllable 1, ballistic emphasis on syllable 2), 'giving some sense of stress on both syllables'; author adds 'Additional research, perhaps using machine analysis would be advisable in this area.'
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD (SIL 67646) describes Kombio [xbi] of the Dreikikir area, East Sepik, with example forms tagged for the Mwi (RL), Wampukuamp (W) and Yanimoi dialects; the stress statement is given for the language as a whole. The dictionary notes one Wampukuamp form (ntamai 'bow') with initial accent against the general final pattern. WALS's Kombio (wals_code xbi) is sourced solely from Yi 2008, which is unavailable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No phonology section of its own (the introduction points to the OPD and its Supplement), but entry-level [Phon:] notes take final stress as the 'typical stress pattern' and flag deviations: an initial-stressed Wampukuamp form ntamai, and a note at p. 20 that the alternation 1st vs 2nd syllable stress on the morpheme ako- 'indicates that stress is environmentally conditioned, not innately'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Transcriptions mark secondary stress on alternating non-final syllables, e.g. sukupel [ˌsu.ku.ˈɸɛl], sukursukur [su.ˌkuɾ.su.ˈkuɾ], ntamimpli [ˌⁿda.mɨm.ˈbli]; one entry says a word was 'written with secondary stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialectal initial stress in ntamai (Wampukuamp); stress shift when -el is suffixed (sukupel); stress 'shifts to second syllable' in an adverbial use of nimiyemp; several entries flagged 'unusual stress pattern' pending analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD (SIL 67646) describes Kombio [xbi] of the Dreikikir area, East Sepik, with example forms tagged for the Mwi (RL), Wampukuamp (W) and Yanimoi dialects; the stress statement is given for the language as a whole. The dictionary notes one Wampukuamp form (ntamai 'bow') with initial accent against the general final pattern. WALS's Kombio (wals_code xbi) is sourced solely from Yi 2008, which is unavailable.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (non-phonemic stress, strong tendency to word-final primary stress, alternating secondaries leftward, rightward shift onto clitics such as -el, pervasive exceptions) rests on the primary fieldworker's own phonology statement (OPD 2011, p.7, quote confirmed verbatim) and her 123-pp grammar sketch (1992, sec. 4.1 p.25, quote confirmed; record locator says p.24, off by one). These are the only first-hand descriptions of Kombio in Glottolog/OLAC; the only unheld 'grammar' (Yi 2008) is an unpublished WALS-sourced sketch. The dictionary downloaded now (418 pp, stress-marked IPA) independently supports final stress as the typical pattern (~72% of marked polysyllables) with many exceptions, matching the exceptions statement='pervasive'. no reclassification needed; optionally fix the Grammar Essentials locator to p.25.

sources.quote: No general stress section in the introduction (it defers to the OPD), but entries carry stress-marked IPA and notes treating final stress as the 'typical' pattern and -el as attracting stress. A rough machine tally of the stress-marked polysyllabic transcriptions in the text layer gives 1818/2528 (72%) final primary stress, 446 penult, 264 other — consistent with 'strong tendency' to final stress with pervasive exceptions.
sources.locator: Entry-level phonetic notes, e.g. p.178 s.v. ntamai [ˈⁿda.mai]: 'Notice the stress change - accent on first syllable here whereas in other dialect and in typical stress patterns, accent would be on last syllable'; p.238 s.v. sukupel [ˌsu.ku.ˈɸɛl]: 'Note that the stress changes when the -el suffix is added'; intro p.7 refers readers to the OPD for phonology.
sources.note: Same fieldworker's 4250-entry dictionary with stress-marked IPA per entry; gives lexical-scale evidence for the 'strong tendency' to final stress and the exception rate behind our 'pervasive exceptions' flag. downloaded now; confirms.
